source.title_on_document: Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort

supplement.where: Supplementary Information appended to the same PDF (PDF pp. 11-41)
supplement.holds: Arm means with SEs and standardized effects with SEs for every study and phase (Tables S6, S7, S12, S19, S20, S28, S29, S34), randomization/balance tables with arm ns (S5, S18, S27), attrition (S4, S17, S26), beta regressions for interview likelihood (S15, S25, S38), rating prompts (S1).

paper_design_summary: Prolific participants took a writing pretest (revising a poorly written cover letter) and a lesson on five plain-writing principles, then were randomly assigned to practice conditions: practice with a custom AI writing tool, practice without it, no practice (Study 2), editor feedback or Google Search (Study 3), or viewing an AI-rewritten example (Study 4). All then rewrote a new cover letter without AI (copy-paste disabled), and Studies 2 and 4 repeated the test one day later. Letters were scored by GPT-4o on adherence to the five writing principles and by lay raters on which letter would more likely earn an interview; Study 1 is a Gallup attitude survey with no task.

eligibility.reason: Studies 2-4 randomly assign about 2,000-3,000 Prolific participants to practice with an AI writing tool, so random assignment and sample size are met. But the task is editing a cover letter to follow five plain-writing principles, and the outcomes are writing quality (GPT-4o adherence index) and lay interview preference. No outcome scores creativity, novelty, or diversity across people, and the task is not a creative or ideation task, so criterion 3 fails (criterion 1 is met only as random assignment of AI, not on a creative task). Belongs to the learning section's scope rather than creativity.

one_line_finding: Practicing with an AI rewriting tool raised later no-AI cover-letter writing quality versus practicing alone (Study 2: 5.01 vs 4.53, d = .38; Study 4: d = .32, Tables S7 and S29, PDF pp. 17 and 36) and versus editor feedback (d = .20, Table S20, PDF p. 28), but the outcome is writing quality, not creativity.
open_questions: Should after-AI writing-quality outcomes from non-creative writing tasks be routed to the learning section instead of creativity screening?
Study 1 N: main text 2,637 vs SI 2,472.
Study 3 editors: 49 in main text (PDF p. 5) vs 44 in SI D2 (PDF p. 25); timing of second session: following day (main text) vs two days later (SI D1).
Table S15 (Study 2) includes a 'See AI example' arm and matches Table S38 (Study 4) in its no-controls column; it appears mislabelled.
Study 4 follow-up count: 633 responders (text), n = 608 (Fig. 8), 72.04% in Table S26 follow-up column.
notes: Forecasting samples (N = 150 each for Studies 2 and 3) predict outcomes and give willingness to pay; they produce no scored output and are not listed as studies. Effort (time, keystrokes, self-reported effort), perceived learning and skill, and feedback requests are process or self-report outcomes and are omitted (Tables S8-S11, S21-S23, S30-S33). Per-principle sub-scores and Claude ratings are treated as robustness variants of the writing-quality index. Arm SDs are not printed; tables give means with SEs and standardized effects with SEs. The candidate record's lead (after-AI writing skill, not creativity) is confirmed. The construct code 'other' is used for the GPT-4o writing-quality index; 'usefulness' for interview likelihood because it judges an output's quality for its purpose.
